834.title: The false sunset
834.hook: a vow with a sunset deadline, and a sun that seems to set too early
834.howItsDone: The day of Jayadratha's death is told in the Drona Parva, and retellings return to the false sunset and Krishna's part in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday Abhimanyu fell inside the wheel, and Arjuna made his vow: Jayadratha before sunset, or the fire. Your line: dharma has rules, even in war. Today, the sun is the clock.

The news of Arjuna's vow reaches Jayadratha in the night, and he wants to leave the war and go home. Drona talks him out of it. Stay, he says, and I'll protect you. So in the morning Drona builds his army into layer after layer, and places Jayadratha far at the back, behind all of it. Arjuna has one day to cut through to a man hidden behind a whole army. Every hour the sun climbs, then starts to fall.
screen: `JAYADRATHA WANTS TO FLEE.` → `DRONA HIDES HIM AT THE BACK.` → `ONE DAY, ONE SUN.`

segments.voice: Arjuna and Krishna drive into the ranks, and the fighting goes on hour after hour. At one point the horses are worn out. In Ganguli's telling, Arjuna stands guard with his bow while Krishna unyokes them and lets them drink and rest, right there in the middle of the battle. But the sun keeps falling, and Jayadratha is still out of reach. Then the light fails. Darkness spreads over the field, and the text says Krishna brought it about by his own power. The Kauravas see what looks like sunset, and they cheer. Jayadratha, safe at last, raises his head to look at the sky. Now, Krishna says. The sun is still up. And Arjuna's arrow takes Jayadratha's head, carrying it into the lap of his father, who had cursed anyone who made it fall to the ground. When the old king rises from his evening prayer, the head drops, and the curse falls on him. The epic doesn't hide the trick, and readers still argue about it. But here's what Hindus who love Krishna hear in this day. Arjuna had staked his life on a vow too big for one man. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells him: declare it boldly, my devotee never perishes. That's bhakti, loving trust in God, and this is its heart: the one who leans on Krishna isn't left alone when his own strength runs out. Many Hindus pray just this way when a day is slipping from them: I've done what I can; the rest is yours.
screen: `WATER FOR THE HORSES` · `DARKNESS BEFORE SUNSET` · `THE SUN IS STILL UP` · then, large: `MY DEVOTEE NEVER PERISHES`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a short prayer for days like this: a name of Krishna, or simply, Krishna, I leave it with you. Think of something you're racing against today. Breathing in, feel how tightly it holds you. Breathing out, say the name or the prayer, and let your hands loosen, the way Krishna watered the horses mid-battle; the race will still be there. If you don't pray, just rest in the out-breath and let what you can't control sit beside you.
Drona. Today he hides Jayadratha behind his whole army, and the hiding place doesn't hold.
Your line: bhakti: my devotee never perishes. Arjuna's vow was too big for one man, and he wasn't alone. Day eight hundred thirty-four, done.

835.title: Karna's one dart
835.hook: Karna has one weapon he can use only once, saved for Arjuna, and in the middle of the night he has to decide
835.carry: dana: he gave even his armor
835.howItsDone: Ghatotkacha is remembered in Hindu storytelling, and in some regional traditions, as Bhima's loyal son; his night battle and death are told in the Drona Parva of the Mahabharata.

segments.voice: Yesterday Drona's army couldn't hide Jayadratha from a false sunset. Your line: bhakti: my devotee never perishes. Tonight the fighting doesn't stop at dark.

Lamps. That's what the field looks like now. The armies are so enraged after Jayadratha's death that they keep fighting into the night, and in Ganguli's telling, lamps are lit on chariots and elephants so the warriors can see one another. Darkness belongs to someone on the Pandava side: Ghatotkacha, Bhima's son by Hidimba, a rakshasa, huge and powerful, and strongest at night. He tears into the Kaurava ranks, and they start to break. Today, the weapon Karna has been saving, and who it finally hits.
screen: `LAMPS ON THE FIELD.` → `GHATOTKACHA, BHIMA'S SON.` → `STRONGEST AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Karna carries a dart called the Shakti, and how he got it is the most famous thing about him. Karna worshipped the sun, and he would not refuse a brahmana who asked him for something. The god Indra came to him disguised as one and asked for the armor and earrings Karna was born with, the ones that kept him from harm. The sun had warned Karna in a dream. He gave them anyway, cutting them from his own body. In exchange, Indra gave him this weapon: it would kill any single enemy, but only once. Karna has kept it for Arjuna. Now Ghatotkacha is tearing the Kauravas apart, and Duryodhana pleads: use it, or none of us will see morning. Karna throws. Ghatotkacha falls, and as he dies, the text says, he makes his body enormous, crushing part of the Kaurava army beneath him. The Pandavas weep for Bhima's son. And Krishna rejoices. The dart meant for Arjuna, he explains, is spent. The epic holds both, real grief and real relief. And look where it all began: with a gift. Hindus still call Karna daanveer, the hero of giving. Dana, giving, is one of the oldest duties in Hindu life, and the Gita calls the purest gift the one given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't repay you, at the right time and place. Karna's gift cost him his armor; tonight it costs Ghatotkacha his life and keeps Arjuna alive. In this epic, a gift is never small.

Breathing in, bring to mind one thing you could give this week to someone who can't pay you back. Breathing out, picture giving it with no strings. If you pray, offer it in your prayer; if not, let the intention settle.

836.title: Ashvatthama is dead
836.hook: Bhima kills an elephant, and then he shouts its name across the field
836.carry: satyam vada: even a half-truth costs
836.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's half-truth about Ashvatthama is told in the Drona Parva, and Hindu storytellers and teachers return to it when they talk about truthfulness, dharma and the costs of the war.

segments.voice: Last night, in Drona's lamplit battle, Karna spent his one dart on Ghatotkacha, and Krishna rejoiced that Arjuna was safe. Your line: dana: he gave even his armor.

There's an elephant on the Kaurava side named Ashvatthama. Same name as Drona's beloved son. Bhima finds the elephant, kills it with his mace, and then turns toward Drona and shouts, loud enough for the whole field: Ashvatthama is dead. It's a trick, and it was planned. Drona has been cutting through the Pandava army, and Krishna has told them, in Ganguli's telling, that the teacher can't be beaten while he holds his weapons. But if he hears that his son is dead, he'll put them down. Today, how a truthful man's half-truth ends his teacher's life.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT NAMED ASHVATTHAMA.` → `BHIMA SHOUTS THE NAME.` → `A PLANNED TRICK.`

segments.voice: Drona hears Bhima, and he doesn't believe it. Not from Bhima. There's one man whose word he trusts: Yudhishthira, known for never telling a lie. So Drona asks him directly. Is my son dead? Arjuna won't have any part of the plan. Krishna presses Yudhishthira: there are times, he argues, when a falsehood saves lives. Yudhishthira is afraid of lying, the text says, and he wants victory. So he answers: Ashvatthama is dead. And under his breath, so Drona can't hear, he adds: the elephant. Then the epic adds a detail. Yudhishthira's chariot, the text says, had always moved a little above the earth. After those words, it sinks and runs along the ground like everyone else's. Drona, his heart broken, lays down his weapons. He sits on his chariot and turns inward, in yoga. Dhrishtadyumna, the prince of Panchala, rushes at him with a sword. Arjuna cries out to take him alive. Too late. Dhrishtadyumna strikes, and the teacher of both houses is dead. Here's what the epic won't let go of. The trick worked, and the war turned. But the man known for his truth paid with the thing he was known for, and the ground itself took note. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students a rule as they leave their teacher's house: satyam vada, speak the truth; dharmam chara, live by dharma. Yudhishthira's words were technically true. Many teachers read the sinking chariot simply: a half-truth told to deceive weighs like a lie. Karna will lead next.
screen: `"IS MY SON DEAD?"` · `"...THE ELEPHANT"` · `DRONA LAYS DOWN HIS WEAPONS` · then, large: `SATYAM VADA: SPEAK THE TRUTH`

segments.voice: Satyam vada: speak the truth. Think of a time you told a half-truth, the true words with the important part said quietly or not at all, and go gently: no need to punish yourself. Breathe in and remember what you said; breathe out and feel how it sat with you afterward, light or heavy. If you pray, you can bring that moment there; if not, just let it be seen.

837.title: Shalya takes the reins
837.hook: Karna takes command, and asks for a king to hold his reins
837.carry: buddhi, discernment, should hold the reins
837.howItsDone: Hindus meet Karna's last battle through recitations and readings of the Mahabharata, retellings, regional theater and television serials; the Karna Parva, the epic's book named for him, tells this part of the war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Drona, the teacher, fell, and your line was satyam vada: even a half-truth costs. Bhishma is down, and now Drona too. So who leads the Kauravas now?

A new commander needs a driver. In the Kaurava camp, Duryodhana turns to his friend Karna and gives him the army. Karna accepts, and then he says something honest. Arjuna has an advantage I don't, he tells Duryodhana, in effect: he has Krishna holding his reins. If I'm to face him, I need a charioteer who knows horses the way Krishna does. And Karna names the man: Shalya, king of Madra, the uncle of the Pandava twins, who ended up fighting on the Kaurava side.
screen: `KARNA TAKES COMMAND.` → `ARJUNA HAS KRISHNA.` → `I NEED SHALYA.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana goes to Shalya and asks, and Shalya is furious. In Ganguli's English, the king takes it as an insult: he, a crowned king, told to drive for Karna, who was raised in a charioteer's house. He nearly walks out of the camp. So Duryodhana talks him round, with an old story of the gods in which the creator Brahma himself drove the chariot for Shiva. Driving, in that story, is no shame. Shalya agrees, with one condition: he'll say whatever he likes to Karna's face. Karna accepts. Now the layer underneath. Before the war began, the epic tells us, Shalya promised Yudhishthira that if he ever drove for Karna against Arjuna, he would wear down Karna's courage with his words. So look at the two chariots. Arjuna's driver is Krishna, steadying him. Karna's driver is a voice in his ear, working for the other side. Hindus have an old picture for this, from the Katha Upanishad. Know the self as the rider, it says, and the body as the chariot. The senses are the horses, the mind is the reins, and buddhi, discernment, is the charioteer. When discernment drives, the horses run true. When it doesn't, the senses bolt like wild horses. Many teachers read the war's chariots through that picture: Arjuna gave his reins to Krishna; Karna handed his to a driver who was never truly his. And the picture leaves you with one old question: who is driving?
screen: `SHALYA TAKES OFFENSE` · `I WILL SAY WHAT I LIKE` · `A PROMISE TO THE OTHER SIDE` · then, large: `WHO IS DRIVING?`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, loosely, like reins held without pulling. Picture the Katha Upanishad's chariot: the senses are the horses, the mind the reins, discernment the driver. Breathing in, notice what's pulling hardest today: your phone, a worry, someone's voice. Breathing out, let discernment take the reins back, gently, with no yanking. If you pray, you can ask God to steady the driver; if not, just let the breath run slow and even.

838.title: The crow and the swan
838.hook: Shalya keeps his promise with a story about a crow and a swan
838.carry: ahamkara boasts; the hamsa flies straight
838.howItsDone: Shalya's fable of the crow and the swan is retold in readings of the Karna Parva and in collections of Mahabharata stories, where it can travel on its own as a story about pride.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna took command, with Shalya at the reins and a promise to the other side. Your line: buddhi, discernment, should hold the reins.

As the chariot rolls out, Karna is in high spirits. Whoever shows me where Arjuna is, he calls across the field, I'll reward him richly. Beside him, holding the reins, Shalya laughs. Save your gifts, he says, in effect. You'll see Arjuna soon enough, and you won't enjoy it. Karna boasts again. Shalya mocks again: two proud men in one small chariot, the army watching. Then Shalya stops arguing and does something sharper. He tells a story.
screen: `KARNA CALLS FOR ARJUNA.` → `SHALYA LAUGHS.` → `A STORY INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, it goes like this. A crow lived in a merchant's house, and the merchant's children fed it the leftovers from their plates. One day some swans came by, and the crow challenged them: I know more ways to fly than you can name. A swan answered simply: I know one way. They set out over the ocean. The crow showed off, diving and wheeling, every trick it knew. The swan flew straight. Far out over the water the crow grew tired, sank toward the waves with nowhere to land, and begged for help. The swan lifted it onto its back and carried it back to land. Then Shalya turns to Karna. You, he says, are that crow, fed on the leftovers of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Arjuna is the swan. The promise to Yudhishthira, kept. Karna answers with hard words and rides on. Shalya meant it cruelly, but Hindus hear more, because the swan, the hamsa, is no ordinary bird to them. The hamsa carries Saraswati, the goddess of wisdom, in countless pictures. An old saying holds that a hamsa can separate milk from water, so it stands for viveka, discernment, telling the real from the false. The greatest saints are even called paramahamsa, the supreme swan. Read in that light, many teachers say, the crow is the other side: ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker, puffed up and showing every trick. Ahamkara gets tired far out over the water. The hamsa needs one way, flown straight, and when the boaster sinks, it lifts him up. So the next time you feel the need to prove every trick you know, the old picture asks: crow, or swan?

839.title: The promise by the river
839.hook: Karna has Yudhishthira beaten, and lets him go
839.carry: vachan: a word kept, even unseen
839.howItsDone: The meeting of Kunti and Karna by the river is retold in readings, plays and poems, and Karna's choice to stay with Duryodhana is discussed in Hindu homes and classrooms as a hard question about loyalty and duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shalya told Karna he was the crow and Arjuna the swan, and Karna rode on anyway. Your line: ahamkara boasts; the hamsa flies straight.

Yudhishthira's bow is cut. His chariot is wrecked. He is the eldest of the Pandavas, the man the whole war is being fought to crown, and he stands beaten, within reach of Karna's weapons. One more arrow would do it. And Karna lowers his weapon. He mocks Yudhishthira, tells him to go back to his own kind and leave fighting to warriors, and he lets him go. In the epic he spares Nakula, one of the twins, the same way. Why?
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA IS BEATEN.` → `ONE MORE ARROW.` → `KARNA LETS HIM GO.`

segments.voice: The answer is back before the war, by a riverbank. Karna used to pray facing the sun, and one day, as he finished, a woman was standing in his shadow. It was Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas. She told him what he had never known for certain: she was his mother too. She had borne him as a girl, before her marriage, a son of the sun god, and set him afloat on the river. Now she asked him to come over to his brothers' side. Karna refused. Where were you, he says in effect, when I needed a mother? Duryodhana stood by me when no one else did, and I won't leave him now. But he gave Kunti something. He promised he would not kill her sons, except Arjuna. One of the two of us will die, he told her, and either way you'll keep your sons. So on the field, with Yudhishthira at his mercy, Karna remembers the riverbank. Here's the part that aches. Karna knows, and Kunti knows, and so does Krishna, who had told him of his birth. To Yudhishthira, Karna is just the enemy who mocked him and let him live. The brothers don't know they are being spared by their own brother. Hindu families have a word for what Karna keeps: vachan, a given word. Tulsidas's Ramayana, sung in many homes, puts it in one line: life may go, but the word must not. Karna keeps his with no one watching and no one to thank him.
screen: `KUNTI AT THE RIVERBANK` · `I WON'T LEAVE DURYODHANA` · `THE BROTHERS DON'T KNOW` · then, large: `VACHAN: A WORD KEPT`

840.title: Arjuna's vow
840.hook: Karna still lives, Yudhishthira lashes out, and Arjuna reaches for his sword
840.carry: dharma upholds life; truth serves it
840.howItsDone: Krishna's stories of Kaushika and Balaka from the Karna Parva are cited in Hindu discussions of dharma when truthfulness and harm pull in different directions, and the brothers' quarrel is retold in readings and serials of the epic.

Wounded and ashamed, Yudhishthira has been carried back to the Pandava camp. Then Arjuna and Krishna ride in from the field, and his face lights up. They've come, he thinks, to tell him Karna is dead. They haven't. Karna is still out there. And the gentle eldest brother, sore from his defeat, turns on Arjuna with words he can't take back. If you can't kill Karna, he says, in effect, give your bow Gandiva to someone who can. Arjuna's hand goes to his sword.
screen: `CARRIED BACK TO CAMP.` → `IS KARNA DEAD?` → `GIVE YOUR BOW AWAY.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, the epic says, had made a secret vow: whoever told him to give his bow to another, he would kill. Now his own brother has said it. Keep the vow, and he kills Yudhishthira. Break it, and he breaks his word. Krishna steps between them and asks a harder question: what is truth, really? He tells two stories. An ascetic named Kaushika had vowed always to speak the truth. Robbers asked him which way some travelers had run to hide, and he told them. The travelers were killed, and the epic says Kaushika suffered for that truthful answer. And a hunter named Balaka killed a creature that was about to destroy all living things, and was honored for it. In Krishna's telling, truth is weighed by what it does to living beings, not only by the letter of a promise. Hindu teachers often explain the word dharma from its root, dhri, to hold up: dharma is what upholds living beings, and truth serves it. Then he offers a way through. For a man like Yudhishthira, he says, to be spoken to with contempt is a kind of death. So Arjuna speaks harshly to his brother, and keeps his vow without a drop of blood. At once he's sorry. The brothers weep, and Yudhishthira blesses him. Then Arjuna rides out again toward Karna, the quarrel healed. This week ends with a family pulled back from the edge.
